title: THE MONARCH OF TELIA: TRACKING WAGDOH'S LAST SHADOW
subtitle: Ballistic pugmark analysis and corridor perimeter survey along the Moharli-Telia boundary buffer.
optics: Sony A7IV · 200-600mm G OSS · 600mm · 1/1000s · f/6.3 · ISO 1600
content: First contact with fresh sign occurred at 05:40 IST along the dry nullah bed bisecting Moharli Compartment 42. Substrate moisture retention was minimal, yet the sheer downward displacement—measured at 28mm into hard-packed sandy loam—could only belong to an apex male exceeding 240kg. Stride length registered at an astonishing 1.62 meters, indicating an unhurried, dominant patrol gait along the territorial boundary.

Acoustic telemetry from the canopy remained dead silent until 06:05 IST, when a solitary chital stag issued two sharp, explosive alarm barks from the edge of the bamboo clump 80 meters northeast. The bark lacked the erratic cadence of a leopard encounter; this was steady, rhythmically paced warning communication signifying a large terrestrial carnivore moving through the understory with deliberate velocity.

Inspecting a mature Terminalia tomentosa trunk revealed fresh territorial claw scoring at an unprecedented elevation of 2.95 meters above grade. Deep vertical grooves sliced through fibrous outer bark down to the pale cambium layer, accompanied by pungent epidermal scent-marking on the lower trunk flank. The sovereign of Tadoba had reaffirmed his territorial perimeter hours before dawn, slipping into the thermal shade of the rocky gorge before midday heatwaves enveloped the forest floor.

title: TELIA LAKE BASIN: DAWN AMBUSH TELEMETRY & QUEEN'S REIGN
subtitle: Multi-point acoustic triangulation of sambar alarm barks across the southern marshline.
optics: Nikon Z9 · 400mm f/2.8 TC VR S · 560mm · 1/1600s · f/4 · ISO 1250
content: Thermal radiation over the Telia reservoir created a low-hanging steam inversion blanket across the water body at dawn. Our GPS stationary point was anchored on the eastern embankment overlooking the emergent Typha grass reedbeds. At 05:32 IST, three adult sambar hind feeding in the shallow marsh snapped their heads toward the dense bamboo thicket on the south levee, ears rigidly cupped forward.

The dominant hind initiated a sustained alarm chorus—resonant, metallic honks that echoed against the sandstone ridge behind the reservoir. Through the 560mm optical assembly, low-profile movement manifested beneath the bamboo canopy: the sinuous, muscular shoulders of an adult tigress advancing in a crouched stalk, staying low enough to submerge her belly hair in the cool muddy shallows without creating surface ripples.

She held position motionless behind a fallen Anogeissus trunk for 18 continuous minutes, displaying absolute predatory discipline. When a juvenile wild boar sounder broke from the reeds at 05:58 IST, her explosive acceleration kicked up a sheet of golden spray. Though the strike missed by inches, the tigress pivoted smoothly onto the bund, shaking the wetland mud from her paws and melting back into the shadows of the southern core.

title: WESTERN GHATS TRANSECT: CANOPY RADIAL GPS & SCRATCH TREE MAPPING
subtitle: Micro-habitat profiling of migratory ridges across the Sahyadri teak transition.
optics: Canon EOS R5 · RF 100-500mm L IS · 450mm · 1/800s · f/7.1 · ISO 800
content: Elevated high along the rugged basalt crest of Junnar transect 11, wind shears gusted at 24 knots ahead of incoming monsoon anvil clouds. This critical wildlife corridor connects fragmented evergreen patches across intense agricultural interfaces. Our objective: log GPS coordinate waypoints for newly identified territorial scent-posts and scratch trees utilized by apex transients navigating the ridge.

At waypoint JG-409 (elevation 684m), a massive Ficus benghalensis trunk bore fresh lateral claw scoring and hair snag samples caught on rough aerial roots. Stereomicroscopic field inspection confirmed thick medullated guard hairs consistent with Panthera tigris. Pugmark impressions preserved in wet basalt silt nearby measured 14.5cm pad breadth, pointing directly down the western saddle toward the river valley.

This transect proves that apex carnivores actively exploit high-altitude ridgelines during adverse weather to bypass human settlements. The corridor remains functionally viable, serving as an irreplaceable genetic conduit between protected core reserves in the northern Sahyadri ecosystem.

title: JAMUNBODI DEEP GORGE: INFRARED TRAIL GRID SENSOR ANALYSIS
subtitle: Sub-surface claw drag telemetry and nocturnal waterhole territorial shift validation.
optics: Bushnell Core DS-4K IR Trail Units // Reconyx HyperFire 2
content: Data retrieval from the Jamunbodi automated sensor grid (Station JB-07) captured 14 consecutive burst sequences between 21:40 and 22:15 IST. Infrared dual-sensor triggers fired as an immense male tiger entered the narrow sandstone defile leading to the perennial spring. The animal's right flank striping pattern confirmed identity: a dominant 9-year-old territory holder extending his patrol radius into the buffer sector.

Sensor telemetry indicated prolonged pause behavior at the rockpool margin. The animal submerged his hindquarters into the cold subterranean seepage for eleven minutes, panting heavily following an uphill ascent through dense Anogeissus scrub. Thermal differentials between tiger body core (38.5°C) and water surface (22.8°C) produced stark, high-contrast monochrome infrared images.

Before departing north towards the Katezhari junction, the male executed five definitive scraping motions with his hind paws on the soft sandstone scree, depositing glandular secretions at the trail bottleneck. This behavioral confirmation proves ongoing territorial assertion and stability along the critical buffer zone frontier.
